title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Multi Region Deployment
summary: Multi region deployment is the practice of running the same application across two or more geographically separated cloud regions so that the system survives a whole-region failure, serves users from the region closest to them…
objectives: What is the difference between active-active and active-passive multi-region, and when would you choose each?
How does asynchronous replication affect RPO, and what does "eventual consistency" really mean in a multi-region system?
What role does DNS play in multi-region traffic steering, and why is TTL critical?
How do you handle data sovereignty in a multi-region system?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Multi region deployment is the practice of running the same application across two or more geographically separated cloud regions so that the system survives a whole-region failure, serves users from the region closest to them for lower latency, and can satisfy data-sovereignty laws that require user data to stay in a specific country.
A "region" in cloud terminology is a fully isolated cluster of data centers — AWS `us-east-1` (Virginia) and `eu-west-1` (Ireland) are 6,000 km apart and have no shared power, network, or control plane. Single-region deployments have an SLA ceiling: even AWS's best regions occasionally fail (the 2017 `us-east-1` S3 outage took down thousands of services for four hours, and the 2021 `us-east-1` outage affected Netflix, Disney+, Slack, and Coinbase). Multi region deployment acknowledges that any one region will eventually fail, and that users in Sydney should not wait 250 ms for a response from Virginia. The architectural commitment is much heavier than multi-AZ: you must replicate data across high-latency links, handle DNS-level traffic steering, plan for conflicting writes, and accept higher cost. The payoff is a system that can plausibly target 99.99% or 99.999% availability — the difference between "four nines" (52 minutes of downtime per year) and "five nines" (5 minutes). Netflix runs active-active across three AWS regions; Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables and Google Spanner are purpose-built databases that make multi-region correctness tractable.

The first architectural choice is active-active versus active-passive. In active-active, all regions serve live traffic simultaneously, all databases accept writes, and replication is bidirectional. This gives the best latency (every user is served from the closest region) and the fastest failover (the other region is already serving, so "failover" is just DNS shifting traffic away from the broken region). The cost is enormous: every region runs at full capacity, data replication is complex, and conflict resolution must be designed into the data model (last-write-wins, CRDTs, or application-level merge). Netflix's streaming service runs active-active on three regions with bidirectional Cassandra replication; Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables replicate writes to all regions within a second. In active-passive, one region serves all traffic (the "primary") and the other is a warm standby that takes over only during a failure. This is simpler and cheaper (the standby runs at maybe 25% capacity), but failover takes minutes (you must promote the standby, repoint DNS, and wait for TTLs to expire) and the standby may have hidden staleness bugs because it has not been serving real traffic. Many enterprises start with active-passive and graduate to active-active as their operational maturity grows.

The second concern is data replication strategy. Synchronous replication (write to region A, block until region B acks) gives zero RPO but adds the inter-region round trip to every write — 50–100 ms between Virginia and Ireland, which kills write throughput. Asynchronous replication returns the write as soon as the local region commits, then ships the change in the background — high throughput but a small window (typically 1–5 seconds) where the secondary lags, so RPO is non-zero. Most multi-region systems use asynchronous replication for writes and accept an RPO of seconds, because the latency cost of synchronous is too high for interactive workloads. The exception is financial systems, where consistency is non-negotiable and Google Spanner's TrueTime mechanism provides synchronous cross-region commits with bounded clock uncertainty. For eventually-consistent data, DynamoDB Global Tables and Cassandra use last-write-wins with clock skew tolerance; for collaborative data (Google Docs), CRDTs allow conflict-free merging without coordination.

The third concern is global traffic steering. DNS is the entry point — services like AWS Route 53, Cloudflare, and NS1 offer routing policies that send each user to the best region. Latency-based routing measures the user's past latency to each region and picks the lowest; geolocation routing maps the user's country to a designated region (required for data sovereignty); weighted routing lets you gradually shift traffic (5% to a new region for canary validation, then 100% if healthy); failover routing monitors a health check and instantly moves all traffic to the standby when the primary fails. The hidden gotcha is DNS TTL: if your records have a 1-hour TTL, a failover takes up to an hour to fully propagate to all clients and resolvers. Production multi-region systems use TTLs of 60 seconds or less (often 5–10 seconds for the global steering record) to keep failover snappy — at the cost of more DNS queries hitting the authoritative servers.

The fourth concern is data sovereignty and regulatory compliance. The EU's GDPR requires personal data of EU residents to be processed under EU law; some interpretations require the data to stay physically in EU data centers. Russia, China, India, and Brazil have similar data-localization laws. A multi-region architecture lets you store each user's data in the region that satisfies the law — an EU user's account lives in `eu-west-1`, a US user's in `us-east-1` — while still presenting a single global application. The complication is that you must shard the user base by residency, not by latency, which means some users will be served from a far region if their country's laws force it. The real-world example: Netflix stores EU subscribers' viewing history in Ireland and US subscribers' in Virginia, with separate DynamoDB Global Tables per residency class.

The fifth concern is the cost trade-off. Multi region roughly doubles or triples your infrastructure bill — two or three full regions, plus cross-region data transfer fees (AWS charges ~$0.02/GB for inter-region traffic, which adds up fast for databases replicating terabytes per day). The decision should be driven by business value: a system whose downtime costs $1M/hour (an exchange) easily justifies multi-region; a content site whose downtime is a minor inconvenience probably does not. Many teams compromise on "two-region active-passive with 30-minute RTO" — half the cost of active-active, but a real DR posture rather than "hope the region stays up." Amazon, Netflix, and Google run multi-region because their businesses are global and downtime is existential; most startups run single-region until they cross a clear revenue or regulatory threshold.

The sixth concern is operational complexity. Multi-region systems are harder to deploy, harder to reason about, and harder to debug. A deployment must roll out consistently across regions (often staggered to catch region-specific bugs); a database bug that corrupts data in one region can propagate to others via replication; a network partition between regions forces a choice between availability and consistency (the CAP theorem in its sharpest form). The mitigation is rigorous tooling: infrastructure as code that treats every region identically, automated DR drills that prove the standby actually works, observability that distinguishes "region A's latency to users in Tokyo" from "region B's latency to users in Tokyo," and runbooks that explicitly cover the partial-failure cases (region A is up but cannot reach region B's database). Netflix's Chaos Kong exercise deliberately fails an entire region every quarter to prove the system survives it; without this discipline, multi-region deployments silently degrade into "two regions that both think they're primary."

The user's browser does a DNS lookup for `app.example.com`; Route 53 evaluates its routing policy and returns the IP of the closest healthy region. 2. The request lands at that region's load balancer, which forwards it to the local app tier — the app reads and writes the local copy of a globally replicated database (DynamoDB Global Tables). 3. The write replicates asynchronously to the other regions within roughly a second; if a region fails, DNS health checks detect it within 10–60 seconds and global traffic steering moves users to a surviving region with no manual intervention.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Multi-region traffic router.

Picks the best region for a given client based on:
  - measured latency (lowest RTT wins)
  - health status (skip unhealthy regions)
  - data-sovereignty overrides (country -> required region)
  - weighted canary (gradual rollout of a new region)

Demonstrates the decision logic that Route 53 / Cloudflare perform
server-side, expressed in plain Python.
"""
import random
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Region:
    name: str
    country: str            # where the region lives
    latency_ms: dict        # client_country -> measured RTT
    healthy: bool = True
    weight: int = 100       # traffic weight for canary/weighted routing

# Sovereignty map: user country -> region that must hold their data
SOVEREIGNTY = {
    "DE": "eu-west-1", "FR": "eu-west-1", "IE": "eu-west-1",  # EU
    "US": "us-east-1",
    "JP": "ap-northeast-1", "AU": "ap-southeast-2",
}

REGIONS = {
    "us-east-1":      Region("us-east-1",      "US",
                            {"US": 25, "DE": 95, "JP": 160, "AU": 180}),
    "eu-west-1":      Region("eu-west-1",      "IE",
                            {"US": 95, "DE": 25, "JP": 200, "AU": 240}),
    "ap-northeast-1": Region("ap-northeast-1", "JP",
                            {"US": 160, "DE": 200, "JP": 25, "AU": 110}),
    "ap-southeast-2": Region("ap-southeast-2", "AU",
                            {"US": 180, "DE": 240, "JP": 110, "AU": 25}),
}

def pick_region(user_country: str, strategy: str = "latency") -> str:
    """Choose the best region for a given user."""
    # 1. Data sovereignty override: if the user's country has a
    #    mandated region, return that region if it is healthy.
    if user_country in SOVEREIGNTY:
        mandated = SOVEREIGNTY[user_country]
        if REGIONS[mandated].healthy:
            return mandated

    candidates = {n: r for n, r in REGIONS.items() if r.healthy}
    if not candidates:
        raise RuntimeError("no healthy region available")

    if strategy == "latency":
        # 2. Latency-based: pick lowest measured RTT for this country.
        scored = [(n, r.latency_ms.get(user_country, 999)) for n, r in candidates.items()]
        scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
        return scored[0][0]

    if strategy == "weighted":
        # 3. Weighted canary: sample proportional to weight (Route 53 weighted policy).
        names, weights = zip(*[(n, r.weight) for n, r in candidates.items()])
        return random.choices(names, weights=weights, k=1)[0]

    raise ValueError(f"unknown strategy {strategy}")

def failover_demo():
    """Simulate a region failure and watch traffic shift."""
    print("== all regions healthy, latency routing ==")
    for c in ["US", "DE", "JP", "AU"]:
        print(f"  user {c} -> {pick_region(c, 'latency')}")

    print("\n== us-east-1 fails ==")
    REGIONS["us-east-1"].healthy = False
    for c in ["US", "DE", "JP", "AU"]:
        # US users no longer sovereignty-bound, fall to next lowest latency
        print(f"  user {c} -> {pick_region(c, 'latency')}")

    print("\n== us-east-1 recovers ==")
    REGIONS["us-east-1"].healthy = True
    for c in ["US", "DE", "JP", "AU"]:
        print(f"  user {c} -> {pick_region(c, 'latency')}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    failover_demo()
```

quiz.explanation: Asynchronous replication returns a write as soon as the local region commits, then ships the change to other regions in the background (typically within 1–5 seconds). The RPO — the maximum data loss measured in time if the primary fails — is therefore the replication lag, not zero. If region A accepts a write at T=0 and fails at T=0.5s before the write reached region B, that write is lost.
